prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow many atoms to be interrogated without light-shift perturbation, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 position and hold it more firmly after the full exchange. Six of eight configurations name B007 with the same two laureates, but I do not rest on that count, which the chair summary rightly says is partly produced by members reading each other's ballots. I rest on the experimental record. The magic-wavelength lattice removes the light-shift perturbation, so many neutral atoms can be probed at once, and that is a different physical lever from the frequency comb (the ruler, 2005) and from single-ion control (a different platform, 2012). Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST, NPL) reproduce fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and agree in cross-comparisons over fibre links, which answers my standing question about independent confirmation. The contribution is decisive and separable: Katori for the concept and the first strontium lattice realisations, Ye for taking the system to the accuracy and stability frontier and for the many-body clock physics. The consequences are already measured and not only promised: height-resolved gravitational redshift at the millimetre to centimetre scale and new limits on drifting constants and on some dark-matter couplings. I answer the chair's question on citation wording directly: the citation should say neutral atoms, magic wavelength and lattice, so that it cannot be read as a prize for optical clocks in general or for the comb or ion control. The wording I propose does that.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains novelty against the 2005 and 2012 prizes: a sceptic can call this a spectacular improvement of an already honoured measurement tradition, and Danielsson is right that it improves a known quantity by many orders of magnitude and does not reveal a new phenomenon. Second, priority outside the pair: Lemonde, Derevianko and Pal'chikov on the magic-wavelength idea and light-shift theory, and the Al+ and Sr+ ion-clock groups, are not credited, and several of us, myself included, are working from recollection of the 2001-2003 record. Third, the SI second has not yet been redefined. On that last point I take a position and do not just list it: waiting is the wrong rule. The prize follows the demonstrated and independently compared science, and the redefinition is a metrology-committee decision that rests on exactly the evidence we already have. The priority question is real, and I would ask that expert reports from outside the committee check the 2001-2003 timeline before the vote is final, but a clean two-name credit with a carefully worded citation is, in my judgment, defensible as it stands.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B012 (IceCube) first with Halzen and Karle, argues the discovery is a clue from nature while the clocks are an instrument, and says he will weigh seriously that B007 is the candidate that can gain a broad majority.
responses.response: I ranked IceCube first myself in the opening and still regard it as the strongest candidate in the list as a discovery about nature, so I do not dismiss your distinction between discovery and instrument. I disagree on where it leads. The prize has always honoured inventions and instruments, and the lattice clock is not only an instrument: the redshift and constant-variation measurements already come from it. I agree with you that the diffuse flux is solid and the source identifications are a bonus. My difficulty is attribution, where we agree on the problem if not on its weight. Halzen and Karle is a sensible pair, but AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal precursors, a collaboration of hundreds and Yoshida's place on the shortlist mean that two names will be contested by the community in a way that Katori and Ye will not. I keep B012 as my first alternative, and I would support it as a second part only if the committee can settle a two-name credit with outside expert help.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B032 (fluctuation theorems) first on grounds of exactness, generality and thirty years of confirmation, concedes the attribution is the real weakness and lists B007 as first alternative.
responses.response: I accept that the theorems are exact and tested, and your confidence in them is something I cannot check from my own field; I rely on you for the physics. The difficulty is the one you name yourself. Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Searles, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert all have credible claims, and the limit of three would force us to say that the omitted four did not do the decisive work. A prize I would not be able to defend to the community is not made safer by exactness. On your second point, whether confirming experiments count as a discovery, I do not think that is disqualifying in itself, but it does weaken B032 relative to a result that was measured and not just verified. If you can show a three-name credit that does not rest on recollection, for instance through an external report, I will read it, but at present I do not move toward B032.

responses.point: Olsson says she can check the first-demonstration versus record-accuracy credit against the record, and notes that Katori's and Ye's groups claim different parts of the story, with Tokyo as an institutional connection she discloses.
responses.response: This is the check I most want done, and I am glad you have flagged that you can do it, because I cannot do it from memory. Please state in the next stage whether the record supports Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice demonstrations, and Ye for the accuracy and stability frontier. If the split is as we all describe it, the two-name credit holds. I also take your Tokyo connection as an institutional disclosure that does not disqualify you, since it involves no collaboration with either laureate. On your point that this is an original invention and not a lifetime achievement, I agree, and I think it is the strongest answer to the novelty objection.

responses.point: Eriksson moved his top choice from B018 (DMFT) to B007 but still feels the pull of condensed-matter candidates B018 and B005 and does not want strong metrology to crowd out condensed matter simply because it has the broadest opening support.
responses.response: I agree that breadth of support should not decide the matter, and I appreciate that you state this. I would ask the same of myself: I moved to B007 because the confirmation and attribution evidence is stronger than for the alternatives, not because six others did. On the condensed-matter candidates, my own concern is the one you identify yourself: the Metzner omission for DMFT and the open pairing mechanism and sample dependence for twisted bilayer graphene. If you want to propose either as a second part, I would need a three-name credit that fits within the overall limit of three people, and with Katori and Ye already taking two names that leaves room for only one more, which I do not think any condensed-matter case on this list satisfies. I therefore do not support a two-part prize this year.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first, argues the magic-wavelength scheme is a distinct enabling idea, and notes that the three-person limit would constrain any second prize part to one extra name.
responses.response: I agree with your framing and with your point that the citation has to carry the distinction. I have made the wording explicit about neutral atoms, magic wavelength and lattice for that reason. Your remark on the three-person limit is decisive for me on the one-part versus two-part question: a second part would have to be a single-name achievement, and nothing on the shortlist has a one-name credit that I would defend. I also note that you and Lindroth are best placed to check the Lemonde and Derevianko record, and I would ask you to say plainly in the final stage whether either needs to be considered for the credit and not leave it among the reservations.

uncertainties: Priority of the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice demonstrations (Katori 2001-2003) against Lemonde, Derevianko and Pal'chikov, and against the early Sr work at JILA, has not been verified from primary records in this process; I rely on colleagues in atomic physics.
Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I think they are, but the outside-reader risk is real.
Whether a defensible two- or three-name credit for IceCube (Halzen, Karle, with or without Yoshida) can be agreed, in case the committee wants B012 as a second part or in place of B007.
AMO and metrology are outside my own expertise; I judge B007 on reproduction, cross-comparison and systematics, not on the detailed atomic physics.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I know of no collaboration with Katori, Ye or the other B007 names; my collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur) are in astroparticle physics. B012 (IceCube) lies in my broad field of astroparticle physics and I know that community professionally, which I flag for information, though my profile shows no collaboration with the credited people. As Chair I have tried to describe the first-round positions fairly, and I have not used the support counts as a scientific argument.
